evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A,B.

source: Surprisingly, application of kainate (KA, 2 µM) in the presence of selective antagonists for AMPA, NMDA and GABA receptors (2 µM NBQX, 50 µM APV and 100 µM PiTX, respectively) induced no or only a very small current (LA: 6 ± 1 pA; BA: 8 ± 1 pA) in the BLA neurons during the first postnatal week (P4-P7), while a marked inward current was observed later on in development (P14-P16) (LA: 81 ± 19 pA, BA 37 ± 5 pA) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In the CeA, a small KA-induced inward current was detected already at P4-P6 (15 ± 2 pA).
source: In the CeA, a small KA-induced inward current was detected already at P4-P6 (15 ± 2 pA), but the current was significantly larger at P14-16 (27 ± 3 pA, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=8.00, p=0.005)(Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The KA-induced current in CeA was significantly larger at P14-16 (27 ± 3 pA) compared to P4-P6.
source: In the CeA, a small KA-induced inward current was detected already at P4-P6 (15 ± 2 pA), but the current was significantly larger at P14-16 (27 ± 3 pA, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=8.00, p=0.005)(Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Application of domoate (500 nM) induced no current in LA neurons at P4-P7 (4 ± 1 pA).
source: Application of domoate (500 nM) induced no current in LA neurons (4 ± 1 pA), but in BA a small inward current was detected (17 ± 1 pA; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Application of domoate (500 nM) induced a small inward current in BA neurons at P4-P7 (17 ± 1 pA).
source: Application of domoate (500 nM) induced no current in LA neurons (4 ± 1 pA), but in BA a small inward current was detected (17 ± 1 pA; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The high expression of the KAR subunits in the newborn LA does not correlate with ionotropic function of KARs.
source: Thus, the high expression of the KAR subunits in the newborn LA does not correlate with ionotropic function of KARs, which emerges after the second postnatal week.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing expression data (Figure 1) with functional data (Figure 3).

claim: Ionotropic KAR function emerges after the second postnatal week in LA.
source: Thus, the high expression of the KAR subunits in the newborn LA does not correlate with ionotropic function of KARs, which emerges after the second postnatal week.
evidence: This is supported by the kainate application data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ACET application resulted in a small but significant increase in the mEPSC frequency in BA at P4-P6 (130 ± 4% of control).
source: In contrast, ACET application resulted in a small but significant increase in the mEPSC frequency in BA at P4-P6 (130 ± 4% of control, signed rank test, Z = 2.93, p=0.004), but not at P14-P16 (92 ± 7%, paired t-test, t(3)=1.11, p=0.35) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with ACET application shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ACET had no effect on mEPSC frequency in BA at P14-P16 (92 ± 7% of control).
source: In contrast, ACET application resulted in a small but significant increase in the mEPSC frequency in BA at P4-P6 (130 ± 4% of control, signed rank test, Z = 2.93, p=0.004), but not at P14-P16 (92 ± 7%, paired t-test, t(3)=1.11, p=0.35) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with ACET application shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ACET application resulted in marked depression of mEPSC frequency in CeA in first postnatal week (P5-6) (73 ± 5%).
source: In CeA, ACET application resulted in a marked depression of mEPSC frequency in first postnatal week (P5-6) (73 ± 5%, paired t-test, t(10)=4.22, p=0.0018) without affecting their amplitude (99 ± 3%).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with ACET application shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ACET had no effect on mEPSCs at P10-P11 CeA (frequency 101 ± 7%).
source: Also this effect was developmentally restricted, as ACET had no effect of mEPSCs at P10-P11 CeA (frequency 101 ± 7%, amplitude 98 ± 4%; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with ACET application shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GluK1 subunit containing KARs are physiologically activated to regulate glutamatergic transmission in the amygdala during the first postnatal week.
source: These data show that GluK1 subunit containing KARs are physiologically activated to regulate glutamatergic transmission in the amygdala during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is concluded from the ACET experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: KAR effect is area and/or cell type specific, with KAR-mediated inhibition and facilitation of transmission at glutamatergic inputs to BA and CeA, respectively.
source: Their effect is area and/or cell type specific, with KAR-mediated inhibition and facilitation of transmission at glutamatergic inputs to BA and CeA, respectively.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of ACET in BA (increase) and CeA (decrease) shown in Figure 4.

claim: ACET application resulted in significant reversible depression of the EPSC amplitude at BLA-CeA pathway at P5-6 (62 ± 5% of control).
source: Consistent with hypothesis that presynaptic GluK1 subunit containing KARs regulate transmission at this pathway, ACET application resulted in significant reversible depression of the EPSC amplitude (62 ± 5% of control, paired t-test, t(7)=-3.586, p=0.009) that was associated with an increase in paired – pulse ratio (PPR) (150 ± 14%, paired t-test, t(8)=4.01, p=0.0039) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by evoked EPSC recording data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ACET-induced depression of EPSC amplitude at BLA-CeA pathway was associated with an increase in paired-pulse ratio (150 ± 14%).
source: Consistent with hypothesis that presynaptic GluK1 subunit containing KARs regulate transmission at this pathway, ACET application resulted in significant reversible depression of the EPSC amplitude (62 ± 5% of control, paired t-test, t(7)=-3.586, p=0.009) that was associated with an increase in paired – pulse ratio (PPR) (150 ± 14%, paired t-test, t(8)=4.01, p=0.0039) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by evoked EPSC recording data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: EPSCs evoked by BLA stimulation were completely blocked by the AMPA-receptor selective antagonist GYKI53655 (8 ± 2% of control).
source: Furthermore, EPSCs evoked by single pulse or paired pulses with 50 ms interval of BLA stimulation were completely blocked by the AMPA-receptor selective antagonist GYKI53655 (25 µM) (8 ± 2% of control, paired t-test, t(7)=-3.679, p=0.008), excluding the possibility that postsynaptic KARs significantly contributed to the eEPSC in this pathway (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Postsynaptic KARs do not significantly contribute to the eEPSC in the BLA-CeA pathway during the first postnatal week.
source: Furthermore, EPSCs evoked by single pulse or paired pulses with 50 ms interval of BLA stimulation were completely blocked by the AMPA-receptor selective antagonist GYKI53655 (25 µM) (8 ± 2% of control, paired t-test, t(7)=-3.679, p=0.008), excluding the possibility that postsynaptic KARs significantly contributed to the eEPSC in this pathway (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the complete blockade by AMPA receptor antagonist.

claim: During the first postnatal week, no postsynaptic responses in CeA neurons to stimulation of external and internal capsulae were observed.
source: However, during the first postnatal week, we could not observe any postsynaptic responses in CeA neurons to stimulation of external and internal capsulae, the regions containing cortical and thalamic projections to amygdala (not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations, though data is not shown.

claim: External inputs to CeA are not present during the first postnatal week.
source: This suggests that external inputs to CeA are not present during the first postnatal week and thus do not contribute to the observed changes in mEPSC frequency in response to KAR antagonism in the neonate (P5-6) CeA.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of responses to external stimulation.

claim: Application of kainate (500 nM) resulted in transient increase in mEPSC frequency in P5-P6 CeA (146 ± 27%).
source: Application of a broad KAR agonist KA (500 nM) and ATPA (1 µM), agonist selective for GluK1 subunit containing KARs, resulted in transient increase in mEPSC frequency in P5-P6 CeA (KA: 146 ± 27%, paired t-test, t(6)=4.24, p=0.0055; ATPA: 191 ± 21%, paired t-test t(6)=3,14, p=0.02; Figure 5C,D), with no effect on mEPSC amplitude (91 ± 8.8% for KA and 100 ± 13% for ATPA).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with agonist application shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Application of ATPA (1 µM) resulted in transient increase in mEPSC frequency in P5-P6 CeA (191 ± 21%).
source: Application of a broad KAR agonist KA (500 nM) and ATPA (1 µM), agonist selective for GluK1 subunit containing KARs, resulted in transient increase in mEPSC frequency in P5-P6 CeA (KA: 146 ± 27%, paired t-test, t(6)=4.24, p=0.0055; ATPA: 191 ± 21%, paired t-test t(6)=3,14, p=0.02; Figure 5C,D), with no effect on mEPSC amplitude (91 ± 8.8% for KA and 100 ± 13% for ATPA).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with agonist application shown in Figure 5D.

claim: GluK1 subunit containing receptors can fully account for KAR regulation of transmission at BLA-CeA synapse.
source: The peak increase in mEPSC frequency in response to ATPA and KA was comparable in size or if anything, slightly larger in ATPA as compared to KA (ANOVA, F(1,12) = 4.50, p=0.055), suggesting that GluK1 subunit containing receptors can fully account for KAR regulation of transmission at this synapse without additional (GluK1 lacking) KAR populations involved.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the effects of GluK1-selective agonist ATPA with broad agonist KA.

claim: ACET had no effect on mEPSCs in P4-P6 CeA in slices preincubated with pertussis toxin (PTX) (108 ± 17% of control).
source: Finally, ACET had no effect on mEPSCs in P4-P6 CeA in slices that were preincubated in presence of pertussis toxin (PTX), a selective inhibitor of the Gαi/o signaling (mEPSC frequency in ACET, 108 ± 17% of control; paired t-test t(4)=1.243, p=0.282; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with PTX preincubation shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ACET application resulted in significant depression of mEPSC frequency in slices incubated under control conditions (72 ± 12%).
source: The incubation procedure itself had no effect on the regulation of transmission by KARs, as ACET application resulted in significant depression of mEPSC frequency in slices incubated under control conditions (72 ± 12%, paired t-test, t(4)=2.934, p=0.043).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: GluK1-subunit containing KARs upregulate glutamate release at immature BLA-CeA synapses via a G-protein coupled signaling mechanism.
source: Together, these data indicate that GluK1-subunit containing KARs upregulate glutamate release at immature BLA-CeA synapses via a G-protein coupled signaling mechanism.
evidence: This is concluded from the PTX experiments and other pharmacological data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Immature-type KAR activity is proposed to be critical for development and fine-tuning of the glutamatergic synapses.
source: Immature-type KAR activity is proposed to be critical for development and fine-tuning of the glutamatergic synapses (Vesikansa et al., 2007; Vesikansa et al., 2012; Orav et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The viral transduction in Grik1 cKO mice covered 79 ± 5% and 61 ± 8% of cells in LA and BA, respectively, and 10 ± 4% of cells in the CeA.
source: The viral transduction covered 79 ± 5% and 61 ± 8% of cells in LA and BA, respectively, and 10 ± 4% of cells in the CeA, based on green fluorescence signal in DAPI labeled cells at P21 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of GFP expression shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Loss of GluK1 in the BLA had no effect on the mEPSCs at LA neurons.
source: Loss of GluK1 had little or no effect on glutamatergic inputs to LA neurons, since there was no significant difference in the mEPSC frequency or amplitude between GFP-CRE and GFP- expressing neurons (frequency 100 ± 9% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,23)=0.0004, p=0.99; amplitude 96 ± 3% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,23)=0.21, p=0.65; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In CeLA neurons, both mEPSC frequency and amplitude were significantly lower in GFP-CRE slices as compared to controls (frequency 38 ± 6% of GFP control; amplitude 73 ± 6% of GFP control).
source: In contrast, in CeLA neurons, both mEPSC frequency and amplitude were significantly lower in GFP-CRE slices as compared to controls (frequency 38 ± 6% of GFP control, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=7.752, p=0.005; amplitude 73 ± 6% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,19) = 10.226, p=0.005; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of mEPSCs in the CeLA neurons was associated with a significant reduction in the spine density (61 ± 12% of GFP control).
source: Post hoc morphological analysis indicated that the loss of mEPSCs in the CeLA neurons was associated with a significant reduction in the spine density (61 ± 12% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,22) = 10.19, p=0.004; Figure 6C) and interestingly, lower dendritic length (54 ± 7% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,19) = 10.41, p=0.004; Figure 6D) and branching (two-way ANOVA, F(19,418)=2,89, p<0,0001; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Loss of GluK1 was associated with lower dendritic length in CeLA neurons (54 ± 7% of GFP control).
source: Post hoc morphological analysis indicated that the loss of mEPSCs in the CeLA neurons was associated with a significant reduction in the spine density (61 ± 12% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,22) = 10.19, p=0.004; Figure 6C) and interestingly, lower dendritic length (54 ± 7% of GFP control, ANOVA F(1,19) = 10.41, p=0.004; Figure 6D) and branching (two-way ANOVA, F(19,418)=2,89, p<0,0001; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Following GluK1 knockout, the spine density and dendritic morphology in CeLA neurons was comparable to those at P10 in wildtypes.
source: These data pinpoint GluK1 in maturation of CeLA but not LA neurons. Following GluK1 knockout, the spine density and dendritic morphology in CeLA neurons was comparable to those at P10 in wildtypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that absence of GluK1 disrupted developmental maturation of the dendritic tree in CeLA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with developmental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Absence of GluK1 disrupted developmental maturation of the dendritic tree in CeLA neurons.
source: These data pinpoint GluK1 in maturation of CeLA but not LA neurons. Following GluK1 knockout, the spine density and dendritic morphology in CeLA neurons was comparable to those at P10 in wildtypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that absence of GluK1 disrupted developmental maturation of the dendritic tree in CeLA neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockout neurons resemble immature wildtype neurons.

claim: Inactivation of GluK1 expression in BLA at P14 had no effect on mEPSCs in CeLA neurons at P35.
source: Consistent with this idea, inactivation of GluK1 expression in BLA at a later developmental stage (BLA virus injection at P14, ex vivo recording at P35) had no effect on mEPSCs (mEPSC frequency: 111 ± 10% of control, ANOVA F(1,15)=0.411, p=0.531; amplitude: 106 ± 7% of control, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=0.454, p=0.50; Figure 6E), spine density (90 ± 8% of control, ANOVA F(1,17)=0.452, p=0.51; Figure 6F), dendritic length (107 ± 8% of control, ANOVA F(1,16)=0.283, p=0.602; Figure 6G) or dendritic intersections (two-way ANOVA F(15,195)=0.7235, p=0.76, Figure 6G) in CeLA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data from later-stage manipulation shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: The stimulus-response relationship of EPSCs evoked by LA stimulation was steeper in control (GFP) slices as compared GFP-CRE group.
source: The stimulus-response relationship of EPSCs, evoked by LA stimulation using fixed intensities, was steeper in control (GFP) slices as compared GFP-CRE group (two-way ANOVA, F(16, 48)=4.54, p<0.0001; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by input-output curve data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The AMPA/NMDA ratio was significantly lower in the GFP-CRE slices as compared to controls (39 ± 8% of control).
source: In addition, the AMPA/NMDA ratio was significantly lower in the GFP-CRE slices as compared to controls (39 ± 8% of control, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=4.973, p=0.026; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by AMPA/NMDA ratio measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There was no difference in the paired pulse ratio between GFP-CRE and control slices (105 ± 18% of control).
source: There was no difference in the paired pulse ratio (105 ± 18% of control, ANOVA F(1,18) = 0.0572, p=0.814; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by paired-pulse ratio data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Loss of GluK1 in the BLA is associated with significantly weaker AMPA-R-mediated synaptic transmission from LA to CeLA.
source: Thus, loss of GluK1 in the BLA is associated with significantly weaker AMPA-R-mediated synaptic transmission from LA to CeLA.
evidence: This is concluded from the evoked EPSC data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: sEPSC frequency was lower in LF neurons in CeLA in animals infected with GFP-CRE encoding AAV viruses at P2-4 as compared to GFP controls (56 ± 5%).
source: We found that developmental loss of GluK1 specifically affected glutamatergic inputs to the LF cell population, where sEPSC frequency was significantly lower in the GFP-CRE slices as compared to GFP controls (sEPSC frequency, 56 ± 5%, ANOVA F(1,22)=5.54, p=0.028; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by spontaneous EPSC recording data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the sEPSCs between GFP-CRE and control groups in the RF cells (95 ± 14% of control).
source: There was no significant difference in the sEPSCs between the groups in the RF cells (GFP-CRE, 95 ± 14% of control, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=1.76, p=0.184).
evidence: This is supported by spontaneous EPSC recording data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Loss of GluK1 weakens glutamatergic projections from LA to CeLA, leading to significant changes in the excitation-inhibition balance in the amygdala circuit.
source: These data indicate that loss of GluK1 weakens glutamatergic projections from LA to CeLA, leading to significant changes in the excitation-inhibition balance in the amygdala circuit.
evidence: This is concluded from the sEPSC and sIPSC data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GluK1 deficiency was associated with a significantly lower E/I ratio in the late firing neurons in the CeLA.
source: Specifically, GluK1 deficiency was associated with a significantly lower E/I ratio in the late firing neurons in the CeLA (sEPSC/sIPSC ratio in GFP-CRE and GFP groups, LF neurons: 9.9 ± 2 and 4.4 ± 0.6, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=4.91, p=0.027; RF neurons: 6.3 ± 2.4 and 4.8 ± 1.7, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=0.48, p=0.488).
evidence: This is calculated from the sEPSC and sIPSC data.

claim: Lentiviral transduction was spatially restricted to LA (59 ± 5% of DAPI-positive cells), with minimal expression in BA (0.7 ± 0.4%) and CeA (0.1 ± 0.4%).
source: In addition, the injected lentiviruses produced a transduction that was spatially restricted to LA (GFP expression as a percentage of all DAPI-positive cells, LA: 59 ± 5%, BA: 0.7 ± 0.4%, CeA: 0.1 ± 0.4%; Figure 8A), thus selectively targeting the presynaptic/axonal GluK1 receptors in the LA-CeA projections.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of viral transduction shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In slices with local lentiviral expression of Grik1 shRNA in the LA, mEPSC frequency in CeA at P10-P11 was significantly lower as compared to controls (38 ± 18%).
source: In slices with local lentiviral expression of Grik1 shRNA in the LA, mEPSC frequency in CeA at P10-P11 was significantly lower as compared to controls expressing a mock shRNA construct (38 ± 18%, ANOVA, F(1,9)=7.59, p=0.02; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with shRNA manipulation shown in Figure 8B.

claim: GluK1 overexpression (oe) in the LA was associated with significantly higher mEPSC frequency in the CeA as compared to GFP expressing controls at P14 (188 ± 38%).
source: Accordingly, GluK1 overexpression (oe) in the LA was associated with significantly higher mEPSC frequency in the CeA as compared to GFP expressing controls at P14 (188 ± 38%, ANOVA on ranks, H(1)=4.77, p=0.029; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC recording data with overexpression shown in Figure 8C.

claim: GluK1 oe in the LA recapitulated the tonic KAR-dependent regulation of mEPSC frequency in the CeA at P14.
source: Importantly, GluK1 oe in the LA recapitulated the tonic KAR-dependent regulation of mEPSC frequency in the CeA at a developmental stage (P14) when this regulation was no longer observed at control or GFP expressing slices.
evidence: This is supported by ACET experiments in overexpression slices shown in Figure 8D.

claim: In slices with LA-specific GluK1 oe, ACET application resulted in a significant decrease in the mEPSC frequency in CeA cells (73 ± 11% of control).
source: Thus, in slices with LA-specific GluK1 oe, ACET application resulted in a significant decrease in the mEPSC frequency in CeA cells (73 ± 11% of control, paired t-test, t(4)=5,496, p=0.0053), but had no effect in control (GFP expressing) slices (103 ± 7% of control, paired t-test t(4)=1,267, p=0.274) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Presynaptic GluK1 KARs, located in the axons of LA principal neurons, regulate glutamatergic transmission to CeA.
source: These results confirm that presynaptic GluK1 KARs, located in the axons of LA principal neurons, regulate glutamatergic transmission to CeA.
evidence: This is concluded from the lentiviral manipulation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The number of dendritic intersections in both apical and distal dendrites was significantly higher in GluK1 oe slices as compared to controls (total dendritic length 200 ± 22% of GFP).
source: In addition, morphological analysis of the CeA neurons indicated that the number of dendritic intersections in both apical and distal dendrites was significantly higher in GluK1 oe slices as compared to controls (total dendritic length in GluK1 oe slices, 200 ± 22% of GFP, ANOVA F(1,11)=22.6, p<0.001; dendritic intersections, two-way ANOVA F(8, 90)=3.014, p=0.0049; Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: No significant differences in the density of dendritic spines were detected between GluK1 oe and control slices (116 ± 7% of GFP control).
source: In contrast, no significant differences in the density of dendritic spines were detected (mean density of spines in GluK1 oe slices, 116 ± 7% of GFP control; ANOVA F(1,14)=1.48, p=0.24; Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by spine density analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Developmental manipulation of GluK1 expression in the LA results in lasting changes in glutamatergic synaptic transmission from LA to CeA.
source: Together, these data indicate that developmental manipulation of GluK1 expression in the LA results in lasting changes in glutamatergic synaptic transmission from LA to CeA and support that presynaptic GluK1 subunit containing KARs are required for appropriate development of intrinsic glutamatergic connections in the amygdala.
evidence: This is concluded from all the manipulation experiments shown in Figures 6-8.

claim: Presynaptic GluK1 subunit containing KARs are required for appropriate development of intrinsic glutamatergic connections in the amygdala.
source: Together, these data indicate that developmental manipulation of GluK1 expression in the LA results in lasting changes in glutamatergic synaptic transmission from LA to CeA and support that presynaptic GluK1 subunit containing KARs are required for appropriate development of intrinsic glutamatergic connections in the amygdala.
evidence: This is concluded from all the manipulation experiments shown in Figures 6-8.

claim: Maturation of the intrinsic and extrinsic connectivity in the rodent BLA occurs postnatally, being completed around P21-P28.
source: Histological and functional evidence indicate that maturation of the intrinsic and extrinsic connectivity in the rodent BLA occurs postnatally, being completed around P21-P28 (Nair and Gonzalez-Lima, 1999; Moryś et al., 1999; Bosch and Ehrlich, 2015; Ryan et al., 2016; Arruda-Carvalho et al., 2017), in parallel with emergence of amygdala – dependent forms of associative emotional learning (e.g. Landers and Sullivan, 2012; Hartley and Lee, 2015; Deal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Maturation of BLA connectivity occurs in parallel with emergence of amygdala-dependent forms of associative emotional learning.
source: Histological and functional evidence indicate that maturation of the intrinsic and extrinsic connectivity in the rodent BLA occurs postnatally, being completed around P21-P28 (Nair and Gonzalez-Lima, 1999; Moryś et al., 1999; Bosch and Ehrlich, 2015; Ryan et al., 2016; Arruda-Carvalho et al., 2017), in parallel with emergence of amygdala – dependent forms of associative emotional learning (e.g. Landers and Sullivan, 2012; Hartley and Lee, 2015; Deal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rapid increase in mEPSC frequency between P5-P10 in CeA reflects mainly formation of the intrinsic amygdala circuits and specifically, development of the BLA-CeA connectivity.
source: However, CeA receives strong glutamatergic input from BLA (Pape and Pare, 2010; Sah et al., 2003), suggesting that rapid increase in mEPSC frequency between P5-P10 reflects mainly formation of the intrinsic amygdala circuits and specifically, development of the BLA – CeA connectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental timing and known anatomy, supported by citations.

claim: The local circuit in the amygdala is wired before the cortical inputs underlying behavior actuate.
source: These data support that the local circuit in the amygdala is wired before the cortical inputs underlying behavior actuate.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the timing of intrinsic circuit development with external input development.

claim: During the first postnatal week, concentration of ambient glutamate is high and sufficient to activate high-affinity KARs.
source: During first weeks of life, concentration of ambient glutamate is high (e.g. Hanson et al., 2019) and sufficient to activate high-affinity KARs (Lauri et al., 2006; Segerstråle et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The developmental increase in glial glutamate uptake provides a plausible mechanism for the decline in the tonic KAR activity.
source: The developmental increase in glial glutamate uptake thus provides a plausible mechanism for the decline in the tonic KAR activity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed developmental changes.

claim: Parallel changes in KAR subunit composition affecting subcellular localization and affinity of the receptors likely contribute to the switch from immature to adult type KAR activity.
source: Parallel changes in KAR subunit composition affecting subcellular localization and affinity of the receptors (e.g. Vesikansa et al., 2012) likely contribute to the switch from immature to adult type KAR activity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of GluK1 and in particular, the GluK1c splice variant, is central to the early metabotropic KAR activity.
source: The previous findings showing coupling of GluK1 to G-proteins (Rutkowska-Wlodarczyk et al., 2015) and recapitulation of immature-type synaptic signaling by GluK1c overexpression (Vesikansa et al., 2012; present data) support the view that expression of GluK1 and in particular, the GluK1c splice variant, is central to the early metabotropic KAR activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and current data.

claim: The high agonist affinity of KARs, permitting tonic activation, depends on availability of subunits GluK4/5 as well as the auxiliary subunits NETO1/2.
source: In addition, the high agonist affinity, permitting the tonic activation, depends on availability of subunits GluK4/5 as well as the auxiliary subunits NETO1/2 reviewed by Lerma and Marques (2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Weakening of glutamatergic transmission at the LA-CeLA projections following GluK1 inactivation was associated with changes in dendritic morphology in the CeLA target neurons.
source: Weakening of glutamatergic transmission at the LA-CeLA projections following GluK1 inactivation was associated with changes in dendritic morphology in the CeLA target neurons, involving reduction in both, the spine density as well as size of the dendritic tree.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Prolonging the developmental KAR activity via GluK1 overexpression resulted in an expansion of the dendritic tree of CeA neurons.
source: Likewise, prolonging the developmental KAR activity via GluK1 overexpression resulted in an expansion of the dendritic tree of CeA neurons, consistent with the idea that KAR activity promotes both functional and morphological maturation of the amygdala neuronal networks.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: KAR activity promotes both functional and morphological maturation of the amygdala neuronal networks.
